p: 11:52 PM, Cocoa Beach. The hotel desk was the kind bolted to the wall, and Sam had the window cranked open so he could hear surf he couldn't see. He opened the scan on his phone.
He knew the page. He'd read it in his first month on the job, on a folding table in Bea's old office, with the heat ticking in the vents. It looked smaller on a phone.

ANOMALY REPORT AR 2207 HALCYON DEPARTURE STAGE SCANNED COPY. ITEM: MAIN OXIDIZER ISOLATION VALVE, MOIV-1. ALDERGROVE FLUID SYSTEMS P/N 7740-112, REV F.. EVENT: ACCEPTANCE TEST, MON AUG 18 2059, CYCLE 3 OF 5. POSITION INDICATION DISAGREEMENT AT CLOSE COMMAND, DURATION 40 MILLISECONDS. CLOSED INDICATION THEREAFTER.. REPRO ATTEMPTS: 2. BOTH NOMINAL.. INITIAL CRITICALITY: 1. REVISED CRITICALITY: 2. RATIONALE: SUSPECTED TEST STAND INSTRUMENTATION NOISE. RECOMMENDED BY: PROPULSION.. FLIGHT RULE 2.36 APPLICABILITY: N/A (CRIT 2).. DISPOSITION: UNR. UNEXPLAINED, NOT REPEATABLE.. CLOSED: FRI SEP 19 2059. APPROVED: B. KOWAL, PROGRAM MANAGER.

It was crooked. Whoever fed it through the copier hadn't squared it up, and the machine had left a gray bar down the left side, an inch wide. For three years somebody had kept this in a drawer, or a box, or a folder with a boring name. Sam stared at the gray bar. Everything else on the page he could have recited.
Forty million people watched Countdown to Ares. Two hundred and twelve of them could watch it from a crater, twenty minutes late. One of those was his.

He got up and closed the window. A minute later he opened it again, for the water. Then he sat back down and started a list on the hotel notepad, in block capitals, of who had to hear it from him before nine Mountain. Nine Mountain was eleven Eastern. He had about eleven hours.
Ruth's Console Log, page eleven: No comment.

Ruth's console log. Petrel. Investigation. L Plus 90 Days. September 10 2035. oh six ten, two vans on the street. one in the neighbor's driveway. the neighbor made them move it. in a robe. oh seven hundred, board, day 90. isol VLV 2 timeline. read my own lines into the record. 0905 wrote clean. ten fifteen, counsel: no comment to press. on advice. all of us. twelve hundred, agency statement. a rigorous process was followed. true. fourteen thirty, the committee cuts next year's mars line by 40 percent. the cargo flight goes. nobody asked us which. sixteen hundred, tate's mother on the news. asked why nobody told the families about the valve. nobody has answered her. nineteen hundred, home. reporter on the step. young. polite. asked if I signed it. nineteen oh one, no comment. nineteen oh two, I signed it. twenty three hundred, garage. telescope. didn't open the case.
I wrote the 1902 line in the kitchen, after the reporter had gone. I meant to say it on the step. That's the whole page, really. The rest is the weather.

By September the Petrel wasn't a ship anymore. It was a story, and the story had its own schedule, and none of us were on it. The investigation board sat every day. The press sat outside my house. The committee that funded us met that afternoon and cut the next year's Mars money by four tenths, and the cargo flight that was supposed to follow the Petrel went with it, and the decision took eleven minutes and nobody asked anyone who'd have known what to keep. And Roz Tate's mother went on the evening news and asked a question nobody at the agency had answered, because counsel had told all of us not to.

What I want you to take from page eleven is simple to say. The outside world doesn't wait for your program to be ready for it. Elections happen on their own calendar. Rules get written by people who've never heard of you. A reporter gets a document. A company you've never met offers to do your job for less. When those things arrive, the project is still yours, and the people attached to it still need the truth from you first. This chapter is about what to do when the outside walks in: how to scan for it, how to tell people, what to do with money that leaves, how to judge an offer, and how every one of those things becomes a change that goes through one door.

How the exam asks it. When the outside world changes something, the exam wants you to assess the impact on the project before you act, and to tell the people affected honestly and early. Silence and spin are both distractors.

The ECO's B8 has three lines, and they're worth learning as a habit rather than a task. Survey changes to the external business environment, and it names the kinds: regulations, technology, geopolitical, market. Assess and prioritize their impact on the project's scope or backlog. And continually review the environment for impacts. The third line is the one people drop. A scan you do once at the start is a photograph of a river.

There's an old tool for this. In 1967 a professor named Francis Aguilar wrote about scanning a business's environment in four categories, political, economic, social, and technological, and people have been adding letters to it ever since. PESTLE adds legal and environmental. The letters don't matter much. What matters is that each category has an owner who'd notice a change in it anyway, because it's their job, and that someone asks each owner, on a schedule, one question: what changed, and does it touch our scope, our backlog, or our risks?

Here's what I'd tell you from experience. Most of the things that blindside a program were published in advance. The election date was on a calendar. The rule had a comment period. The competitor flew its prototype in public. Only a few surprises are really surprises. The rest are things nobody was assigned to read.

When something does change, the order is the same as for anything else. Find out exactly what changed, from the source, not from the headline. Assess what it does to the work: which deliverables, which backlog items, which dates, which risks. Prioritize by value. Then bring it in through change control and tell the people who need to know. On an adaptive project the backlog absorbs a lot of this naturally; the product owner reorders it. On a predictive one it means a change request against the baseline. Most real projects do both.

How the exam asks it. For an external change (a new regulation, a market shift, an election): survey and confirm what changed, assess and prioritize its impact on scope or backlog, then process it through change control. Ignoring it or racing to avoid it are distractors.
When the story is already out.

Sooner or later somebody will hand a reporter a document about your project, and you'll have a few hours' notice, or none. You can't un-leak it. What you control is who hears it from you, in what order, and whether what you say is true.

Start by analyzing the stakeholders, quickly and honestly. A useful tool for a morning like that is the salience model. Its authors sorted stakeholders by three things: power, the ability to make the project do something; legitimacy, a rightful claim on it; and urgency, a claim that can't wait. Someone with all three is definitive, and comes first. Someone with power and legitimacy but no urgency is dominant: they expect to be told properly, on time. Power and urgency without legitimacy is called dangerous, which is unkind but accurate about how a crowd or a hostile outlet can behave. Legitimacy and urgency without power is dependent, and that's where families usually are. Dependent stakeholders lean on someone with power to be heard. Often, today, that's the press.

The power and interest grid is the older, simpler map. High power and high interest, manage closely. High power, low interest, keep satisfied. Low power, high interest, keep informed. Low on both, monitor. Neither picture is the truth. Both are ways of making sure you don't forget anyone at three in the morning.

Then the order. Tell the people whose lives are attached to the project first: the crew who'll ride it, the families of the people it's for. Tell the people named in the document before they read their own names. Tell your sponsor and your governance before the public, so the people who'll be asked about it aren't surprised, and agree the facts with them. That isn't asking permission to tell the truth. It's making sure there's one set of facts and everybody has it. Then answer the press, on the record, with what happened, what's known, what isn't, and when you'll know more.

How the exam asks it. When bad news is about to become public: tell the most affected stakeholders and the sponsor first, agree the facts, then respond publicly with accurate, complete information. Waiting for legal review or the next scheduled update is the distractor.
What the Code says about spin.

The honesty chapter of the Code opens with a sentence I wish I'd had on a card in my pocket in 2035. Honesty is our duty to understand the truth and act in a truthful manner both in our communications and in our conduct.

Read the mandatory standard slowly, because every phrase in it is a technique somebody uses. 5.3.1: we don't engage in behavior designed to deceive others, including making misleading or false statements, stating half truths, providing information out of context, or withholding information that, if known, would render our statements misleading or incomplete. The comment beside the mandatory standards is shorter and sharper: half truths and non disclosures intended to mislead stakeholders are as unprofessional as affirmatively making misrepresentations.

So a statement that a closed anomaly is history, issued the week the valve did it again, fails the standard even if every word in it would survive a lawyer. So does a statement that something is performing within its limits, when the one thing people are asking about isn't. The aspirational side asks more: accurate information in a timely manner. The comment says that includes the courage to share bad news even when it may be poorly received. When outcomes are negative, we avoid burying information or shifting blame to others.

Three smaller lines matter on a morning like that. 2.2.5: when we discover errors or omissions, ours or anyone's, we communicate them to the appropriate authority as soon as they're discovered. 3.2.6: we avoid spreading false or unconfirmed information, which includes the guess about who leaked it. Don't hunt the source in public, and don't name anyone you can't prove. And 4.3.1: if you have a real or potential conflict of interest, disclose it before someone else does. If your daughter is on the station, say so. Everyone's going to know anyway. Let them hear it from you.

"No comment" isn't a lie. I know, because it was the sentence I hid behind. But it left Roz Tate's mother to ask her question on television, and it left a young reporter to write the story without me, and the story that got written was fair, which was worse.

How the exam asks it. A statement that's true in every word but misleading as a whole is a half truth. The honest answer gives the complete picture, including what's unknown, even when it's unflattering.

Budget and funding are different things, and the difference matters most the week a partner walks away. The budget is what the work is planned to cost, time phased, plus the reserves. Funding is the money that actually arrives, when it arrives. A program can have a perfectly good budget and run out of cash in March.

The tool is called funding limit reconciliation. You lay the planned spending beside the limits on the money you can commit, period by period, and look for the places where they don't match. The PMBOK Guide's own fix for a mismatch is to reschedule work so the spending levels out. When the limit drops, the reconciliation tells you which month hurts, and by how much. That's the analysis. The decision belongs to governance, and you owe it options: move work to later periods, take work out by value, or replace the money. Usually some of each.

Then there's the reserve, which people reach for first because it's right there. Remember the two kinds. Contingency reserve usually sits inside the cost baseline, for the risks you've identified. Management reserve is set aside on top of the baseline for the things nobody saw coming, and it's typically released by senior leadership, which on this program means the sponsor and governance. A partner cutting its contribution is a funding problem, not an unknown unknown inside your scope. Using the reserve to cover it might be the right call, and it's the sponsor's call to make. Before anyone makes it, quantify what the reserve still has to cover. Show them what's left after the draw. Most people will decide well if you hand them the subtraction.
In 2035 nobody did the subtraction for the committee. They cut forty percent in eleven minutes, and the cargo flight went because it was the biggest line, not because it was the least valuable.

How the exam asks it. When funding drops: reconcile planned spending against the new funding by period, identify where it falls short, and give the sponsor options (rephase, rescope, replace). Don't cut across the board or draw reserves on your own authority.

Economists have a name for the money you've already spent: a sunk cost, a sum paid in the past that should no longer matter to decisions about the future. Only the costs still ahead of you are relevant. It's called the bygones principle. Everybody agrees with it, and almost nobody follows it under pressure.

It cuts both ways, which is the part people miss. "We've spent two billion, we can't walk away now" is the sunk cost fallacy. So is "we've already sunk two billion into a money pit, so switch to the cheap one." Both arguments are about the past. The honest comparison is what each option costs from here, against what each one delivers.

And what it delivers is the question that usually decides it. The ECO's R3 asks you to examine the business value throughout the project, to evaluate delivery options against the value they demonstrate, and to verify there's a system in place to measure the benefits. A project exists to produce a benefit, and the benefit has a shape: a number, a date, a condition. If the cheaper option doesn't produce it in time, its price is irrelevant, because it buys nothing. A make or buy decision works the same way. Buy is cheaper only if what you buy does the job.

That doesn't mean you ignore an offer like that. Look at it properly, write down why it doesn't fit this need, and ask whether it fits another one. A company that can't save a colony this year might be exactly who you want resupplying it later.

How the exam asks it. When comparing options mid project, ignore sunk costs and compare cost to go against the value each option delivers. An option that misses the benefit isn't cheaper at any price.

Every thing that walked in from outside in this chapter becomes a change. The rule changes the lander's work. The funding changes the time phased budget. The anomaly changes the flight procedure. Each one goes through the same door.

A change request is written down with its schedule and cost impacts, and a designated person or a change control board approves it, defers it, or rejects it, then documents and communicates the decision. The ECO's B3 adds the parts people skip: communicate the status of proposed changes, implement approved changes, and update the project documentation to reflect them. A change isn't done when it's approved. It's done when the plan, the drawings, the procedures, and the people all reflect it.

Two traps. The first is the senior person who approves a change on the phone because it's obviously right. Maybe it is. It still goes through the door, because the door is where the impact on everything else gets looked at, and because some changes alter a risk that only a particular body can accept. The second is the team that improves something on its own because the data suggested it. On an adaptive team, the backlog can change freely, and the product owner decides what's next. But the moment work touches a baseline that governance approved, especially safety critical work, a good idea becomes a proposed change. Write it up. Let it be decided. Then build it.

How the exam asks it. Only approved changes get implemented. An unapproved change found in the work is removed, documented, and submitted as a proposed change; the documentation is updated to match what was approved.

After a month like the one you're about to have, you'll have a dozen changes, each approved in its own room, each right on its own. The integrated plan is the only place where they meet, and that's where they collide. R1 asks you to maintain it, and to assess the consolidated plans for dependencies, gaps, and continued business value.

Dependencies are the same four technicians wanted in two places in the same week. Gaps are the training that moved to after the people who needed it had left. Continued business value is the last question, and the one nobody asks out loud: with everything that's changed, is this still worth doing? Answer it with the measure the project exists for. Then put a version number on the plan and a change log in front of it.

And when a change costs you days you don't have, you know the tool from page three. Crash the critical path where the cost per day is lowest, and leave the tests alone even when they're cheaper, because a test you shorten stops telling you the truth.
How the exam asks it. When several changes are approved, integrate them into the project management plan, check for new dependencies and gaps, and confirm the project still delivers its value.

The reporter on my step wrote about the Petrel for twenty years, and was fair every time. I never gave them an interview, and they never held it against me in print, which I've come to think was a kind of mercy I didn't earn.

You'll have your own morning with your own scan on a phone. Make the list before you make the statement. Call the people with the most at stake while they're still asleep. Then say what's true, all of it, including the part with your name in it. You can live with a bad story. What I couldn't live with was the 1902 line.
How the exam asks it. Under media pressure the best answer is the transparent one, in the right order: most affected stakeholders and governance first, then the public, with what's known and unknown.
Friday, October 6. 12:20 AM. Greaves had asked for his account, politely, which from Greaves meant the segment would run either way and it was up to Sam whether he was in it.

The scan had come with a note, typed and unsigned, one paragraph. This was closed eleven days before a schedule review. It was reopened in 2061 by the people running Halcyon now. Ask them what they've done with it since, and ask them about this week.
It was true. He'd read the record in his first month and gone carefully around it, and in April Hana had reopened it herself, after the valve did it again on the stand.

Two names were on the page. B. KOWAL, who cut keys at a hardware store in Strasburg now and had asked him once not to make her testify. And PROPULSION, which anybody in the business could read as one person. Hana's name wasn't on it. It wouldn't take Greaves long.

The list on the hotel notepad had six lines. Commander Haddad, who'd ride the departure burn on that valve, asleep in a Houston hotel, with four kids and a husband in Aurora. Frances Odum, with two hundred families and a phone that would start at seven. Hale's office, which opened at seven Mountain, nine his time. The board's duty member, who had a number for nights like this. Hana. Bea.
At 12:31 Garrett texted. Say nothing. Lawyers at 7.
A. Tell the crew, Frances, Hale, the board, Hana, and Bea before nine, then give Greaves the facts on the record, known and unknown.
B. Give Greaves a statement that AR 2207 is history from 2059 and that the stage in orbit is performing within its limits.
C. Decline comment tonight and send Greaves to the ARA's public affairs office, which speaks for the program on leaked records.
D. Call Greaves back tonight and give him the whole account on the record now, so the segment at nine has the truth in it.

He calls Haddad at 12:40 and wakes her, and tells her what's coming and what it is and what it isn't. Then Hana, who's awake anyway. Bea at nine, seven in Strasburg, before the store opens. She listens to all of it and says, Thank you for calling me first. Say what's true. I'll stand behind it. At 9:05 he's on with Hale's chief of staff and the board's duty member together, with one page of facts, and Hale's office agrees he'll speak for the program on them. Frances gets a call at 9:30 and her committee an email at 9:45, in the same words. At 10:15 he calls Greaves's desk and gives eleven minutes on the record: when it closed, who signed, what the rule says, what's been done since, what happened on orbit this week, and what nobody knows yet. He tells Greaves his daughter is on the station before Greaves can ask.

That's a go. Analyze who's affected and engage them in order: the crew, the families, and the people named before the public; the sponsor and governance so there's one set of facts. Then answer the press on the record, with what's known and what isn't.

At nine Mountain Greaves ran it straight: the record, the rule, and Sam's eleven minutes cut to four, with the line Sam had known he'd keep. It was closed when it shouldn't have been. It's open now, and I'll tell you what we find when we find it.

At 12:36 PM Eastern, in the hotel room with his bag half packed, the two note chime. One way nineteen minutes and eighteen seconds. She'd watched it with the station, twenty minutes after everybody on Earth, and recorded before he could say a word.

A log from Ada Okafor, Ares Station. Sol 4135. One way, 19 minutes 18 seconds. Margin, 326 days. Hi, Dad. Log forty three. Sol 4135. We get Greaves here, twenty minutes behind you, on the galley screen. Half the station watched it with breakfast. You looked like you. Malik got a message from his mom at five in the morning our time, before any of it aired, and all it said was Sam called me first. He showed me the screen. Then I watched you tell forty million people something was closed when it shouldn't have been, and you didn't do the voice once. Okonkwo said, he talks like an engineer. From her that's a medal. Medals are still a fire code violation, so I'm keeping it for you. The arm's better. The dressing's down to a sleeve, and the ribs only hurt when I laugh, so Malik's been trying. Mom's watch is back on my wrist. Still on Aurora time. Okonkwo's log and mine agree with the board now, give or take the ration cut. Mine says 326. Theirs says 333. Arrival's day 335. Same minus nine. Their minus two. The other place is coming along. I'm not putting it in my number until it's real. Call me back when you can. Not the feed. You. Log forty three. Ada out.
He watched it twice. Then he flew home the next morning.

Tuesday, October 10. 10:00 AM. The conference room at Watkins with the window that looked at the wind sock, which was straight out. Since the broadcast, four groups had asked him, separately and in writing, for four different things.

Hale's office wanted every program statement to go through ARA public affairs, with forty eight hours of review. Garrett's office wanted nobody at Tallgrass to give an interview until launch 3 had flown. Frances wanted a weekly briefing for the families with the same facts the board got, and for the colonists' own messages home to stay unread by anybody else. Commander Haddad, from a screen in Houston, wanted the crew to hear anything about the stage before anyone outside the program did. And Greaves had asked for a standing weekly interview, which Sam had told him he'd answer today.
A. Hold to Garrett's rule of no interviews until launch 3 has flown, so nothing else leaks while the program is under this pressure.
B. Adopt Hale's office's rule for everyone, so every statement goes through ARA public affairs with forty eight hours of review.
C. Give each group the channel and the cadence it asked for, separately, so every one of them leaves today getting what it wanted.
D. Bring them into one room, get each group's expectations said out loud, and agree on one set of facts and when it goes out.

It takes the morning. He asks each of them what they need and why, and writes it on the whiteboard in their words. Under all four, it turns out, is one thing: nobody wants to learn something from the feed again. So they agree on that. The board gets the facts first and the crew the same hour, the families the same day, the public the day after, in the same words. Hale's office reviews for accuracy in four hours, not for tone. Frances gets a weekly call with whoever owns the answer, Sam or Hana or Quinn, and the colonists' messages stay theirs. Only named people speak for Tallgrass, which Garrett can live with. Greaves gets the same weekly note the families get, a day later, and says that's fair. Haddad reads the whiteboard from Houston. Write the crew line in pen.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Aligning expectations means categorizing the stakeholders, finding out what each one actually expects, and facilitating a discussion that lands on terms they all accept. The agreement is the deliverable.

Wednesday, October 11. Page eleven had been on the mat when he got home on Saturday, green ink, Golden postmark, mailed before any of it aired. He'd read it at the kitchen table and then sat for a long time with the 1902 line.
At nine Hana brought the root cause team's answer to the room, which was two answers. She'd written them on one page because she said she wanted nobody to be able to read one without the other.

I-62-117 MOIV-1 ON ORBIT CANDIDATE RESPONSES ROOT CAUSE TEAM OCT 11 2062. 1. REPLACE MOIV-1 BY SPACEWALK. NEW VALVE FROM ALDERGROVE'S NEXT LOT, BUILT AND ACCEPTANCE TESTED BY DEC 20, FLOWN UP WITH THE CREW JAN 9. TWO EVAS AND A RETEST: 9 DAYS OF CREW TIME BETWEEN CREW LAUNCH AND DEPARTURE. ABOUT $41 MILLION ALL IN. DOES NOT NEED THE ROOT CAUSE FIRST. RISK: EVA ON A LOADED STAGE.. 2. FLY MOIV-1 WITH A WORKAROUND. A CONDITIONING CYCLE BEFORE CUTOFF, AND MOIV-2 DOWNSTREAM COMMANDED CLOSED AT CUTOFF AS A SECOND BARRIER. FLIGHT SOFTWARE AND PROCEDURE CHANGE, VERIFIED ON THE GROUND. ABOUT $3.2 MILLION. NO CREW TIME. ROOT CAUSE STILL OPEN.. 3. LONG LEAD: FOR OPTION 1 TO EXIST AT ALL, ALDERGROVE MUST START THE LOT BY MON OCT 23. LOT START $6.0 MILLION.. ROOT CAUSE STATUS: OPEN. CANDIDATES ON THE LIST INCLUDE SEAT WEAR, THERMAL STATE AT CYCLE 3, AND THE POSITION SENSOR HARNESS (REV C ON MOIV-1, REV D ON THE DRAWING). NONE CONFIRMED.

The data sat beside it: June at Watkins under four milliseconds, hot fire 2's seven at the Cape, forty on orbit. Aldergrove's bench in Pueblo had started cold cycles on the same lot the day after the event and hadn't shown anything yet.

Garrett had come out for it. Two. Announce it today. It costs nothing, it doesn't touch the crew, and it's a story with an ending, which this week we could use. Hale's chief of staff, on the speaker, wanted a decision before the partners met on the 18th. Hana didn't look at either of them. I'd like that valve off my stage. I'd also like to know why it did it. Option one gets me the first and not the second.
Nell Garrity had called within the hour of seeing the page. We can start the lot Monday. Tell me if you want it.
Wendell, at the window, said one thing. Option two flies the question.
A. Hold every change to the stage until the root cause team has found the cause, so nothing done now can disturb the evidence.
B. Have Aldergrove start the new valve lot now, so a spacewalk stays possible, and take the choice between them to the board after.
C. Approve the workaround today on Garrett's authority, since it costs no crew time and the software team could begin it tomorrow.
D. Put both responses in one change request with each one's effect on scope, schedule, cost, and risk, and send it to both boards.

Quinn writes it as CR 62-311 that afternoon: both responses, what each changes in the scope, the schedule, the cost, and the risk, and a third line nobody asked for, the cost of keeping both open until December, which is Aldergrove's 6.0 million to start the lot. The change board takes it Monday and sends it up, because accepting the risk isn't the change board's to do. The readiness board sits on Thursday, October 19, and its decision fits on a page: develop and verify the workaround on the ground, authorize Aldergrove's lot so the spacewalk exists, and choose between them at the board's December session, on the data. Sam posts the status that night in two sentences, approved in part, and Frances reads it before Greaves does. The minutes have one line from the bench. MEMBER CALDER ASKED WHO DECIDES IF THE DATA ARE NOT IN BY DECEMBER. THE CHAIR: THIS BOARD.

Exactly right. Execute the change control process: document the change, analyze its impact on every part of the plan, route it to the people with the authority (here, accepting the risk belongs to the board), and communicate its status once it's decided.

Sunday, October 15. One of the eleven partner governments held a general election. Quinn had it on the program calendar, in pencil, because Hale's office had mentioned it in June. By Monday morning the government that had signed the ARA's founding agreement was out, and the one coming in had campaigned on, among other things, a television segment it had watched on a Friday.
Wednesday, October 18. The letter came to the Partner Finance Committee at 4 AM Mountain and to Sam at 4:06.

ARA PARTNER FINANCE COMMITTEE NOTICE FROM PARTNER 09 WED OCT 18 2062. THE GOVERNMENT WILL HONOR ITS SHARE OF THE NOVEMBER 1 TRANCHE, WHICH IS ALREADY APPROPRIATED.. IT WITHDRAWS ITS SHARE OF THE FEBRUARY 1 AND MAY 1 TRANCHES PENDING A REVIEW OF THE PROGRAM'S MANAGEMENT, CITING RECENT REPORTS OF THE PROGRAM'S HISTORY.. PARTNER 09'S SHARE OF EACH TRANCHE: 10 PERCENT.
Ten percent of the last two tranches was sixteen million dollars. It wasn't much against a ship. It was a great deal against a launch quarter.

Garrett called at seven. Cut the autonomy work and the extra ground runs today. Show them discipline before they ask for it. There was autonomy work in Rafa's backlog that had never been made a declared option, a few epics nobody quite owned. The extra ground runs were the workaround's verification, which the readiness board would rule on tomorrow.
Hale called at eight from a car. I'm in their capital next Tuesday. I need to know by Friday what this does to the program, and what I can offer them that isn't an apology.
A. Cut the autonomy work and the extra ground runs today, to show the partners the program can live inside the smaller number.
B. Work out what the cut touches in scope and backlog with the leads, rank it by value to the window, and give Hale options by Friday.
C. Have Quinn model the lost money against the spend plan and send Hale the numbers, leaving the scope questions to the partners.
D. Go on Greaves's feed to answer the new government's charge directly, since it was made in public and the program has to be heard.

Quinn, Rafa, Hana, and Corinne spend Thursday at the whiteboard with the backlog and the work packages, and sort everything left into three piles: what the window needs, what the colony needs after arrival, and what can wait or go. The second pile is the biggest: the station's twenty year spares plan, the lander's surface science package, two of Rafa's crew display epics. Nothing in the first pile is touched. On Friday Sam sends Hale a page: what sixteen million is, which work it would move or cut and in what order, and what each choice does to the launch, the colony, and the risk. Hale reads it in the car to the airport and calls from the curb. This I can carry into a room.

That's a go. When the external environment changes, find out exactly what changed, assess its impact on the scope and backlog, and prioritize by value. Then give the people who decide ranked options before anyone cuts anything.
Monday, October 23. 7:30 AM. Hale had flown out with Friday's page in her bag. Osterhout's office wanted the program's funding plan for the committee's call on Friday.
Quinn had the numbers on one sheet, the way she liked them, in pencil first.

HALCYON FUNDING AND PLANNED SPEND NOV 1 2062 TO CLOSEOUT MILLIONS. CASH CARRIED INTO NOVEMBER: 12. TRANCHE NOV 1: 150 (PARTNER 09 PAYS ITS SHARE). TRANCHE FEB 1: 110, NOW 99. TRANCHE MAY 1: 50, NOW 45. PLANNED SPEND NOV TO JAN: 160 (LAUNCH 3, CREW LAUNCH, ON ORBIT ASSEMBLY). PLANNED SPEND FEB TO APR: 110 (DEPARTURE, CRUISE OPERATIONS, GROUND CLOSEOUT). PLANNED SPEND MAY TO CLOSEOUT: 40
It's fine until it isn't, she said. And when it isn't, it's the quarter with the burn in it.

Garrett's position was in an email: spend to plan and let the ARA sort out the money, because nobody runs a launch campaign on a funding limit. Hana's was in a sentence, at the door. Don't let anyone take it out of the ground runs.
A. Move nine million of February's work to after launch on his own authority, to stay inside the limit, and let Hale know afterward.
B. Trim every remaining control account by the same share, so that no single team carries the cut alone and the totals come out.
C. Lay the new funding beside the spend plan, period by period, show where the cash runs short, and give Hale ways to close it.
D. Keep spending to plan and let the ARA find the money before February, since a launch campaign can't be run to a funding limit.

By Wednesday it's on one page. The cut is sixteen million. Through January the program is two million to the good. By the end of April it's nine short, in the quarter with the burn in it, and at closeout four short. Sam gives Hale three ways to close it, with what each costs. The other ten partners cover the sixteen between them, about eleven percent more on each of their last two tranches. Or nine million of ground closeout work moves from February to after April, which fixes the cash and not the total. Or four million comes out of the second pile for good. He recommends the first, with the second as a bridge. Osterhout reads it and says it's the first program this year to bring him a shortfall with its own month on it.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Funding limit reconciliation compares planned spending with the funding available in each period to find where they don't match. Then you work with governance on the options: rephase, rescope, or replace the money. The sponsor decides.
Wednesday, October 25. 9:00 AM. Osterhout called the program room himself, which he'd never done. He had Quinn's page in front of him and he said so.
Mr. Okafor. You have seventy two million of management reserve, undrawn, in the agency's account. Partner 09 has taken sixteen. I could have this closed by lunch. Tell me why I shouldn't.

It was true. The reserve had sat untouched since the baseline, through a blizzard and a hurricane and a valve. Quinn slid a sheet across the table without being asked: CR 62-311's spacewalk path, about forty one million all in, if the board chose it in December. Six of that, Aldergrove's lot, had already come out of the launch campaign's contingency. No work package carried the other thirty five. If the spacewalk came, that came out of the reserve.
Garrett, copied on everything, had already replied. Take the deal.
A. Move sixteen million out of the reserve into the program's contingency line now, quietly, where the program controls it.
B. Agree to draw the sixteen, with Hale's written approval, since releasing management reserve is the sponsor's decision to make.
C. Refuse to discuss the reserve at all, since it's held for unknowns and a comptroller has no business asking how it'll be used.
D. Show what the reserve may still need to cover, the spacewalk first, and ask the partners to fill the gap before it's drawn.

He puts it in numbers on the call. Seventy two undrawn. If the board chooses the spacewalk in December, about thirty five of it goes there, on top of the lot already paid for. That leaves thirty seven for whatever four months of launch bring, on a program that has met something it didn't plan for about once a quarter. Draw sixteen for the partner and it's twenty one. Sir, the reserve is for the thing we haven't met yet. The partner is a thing we've met. I'd ask the other ten first. Osterhout is quiet long enough that Quinn checks the line. Put that on paper. I'll take it to the committee with my name next to yours.

Exactly right. Manage reserves for what they're for. Quantify the risks still ahead against the reserve, show the sponsor what a draw would leave, and keep a funding problem in the funding process unless governance decides otherwise.
Friday, October 27. The letter had gone to Osterhout on Thursday, copied to Hale, and by Friday morning everyone had read it except, it seemed, the people who'd have to fly it.

KITTIWAKE ORBITAL OFFER TO THE ARES RELIEF AUTHORITY THU OCT 26 2062. WE PROPOSE TO CARRY THE BREATHER AND ITS LANDER TO MARS ON OUR CARGO TUG, UNCREWED, DEPARTING IN THE 2063 WINDOW ON A MINIMUM ENERGY TRANSFER OF 259 DAYS.. FIXED PRICE: $185 MILLION, INCLUDING LAUNCH.. OUR TUG HAS FLOWN TWICE IN EARTH ORBIT.. WE BELIEVE THIS OFFERS THE PARTNERS A SUBSTANTIAL SAVING AGAINST THE COST OF COMPLETING HALCYON.
Osterhout had written one line under it, by hand, and photographed it. 185 against 310. I'm paid to notice that.
Garrett had come to the program room to say his part in person. We've put two point three billion into this ship. We are not walking away from that for a discount.
Quinn hadn't said anything. She'd written two dates on the whiteboard, small, in the corner: February 18 and September 4.
A. Turn it down on the spot because the program has already spent over two billion dollars, which a switch now would simply waste.
B. Ask Kittiwake for a faster transfer and a lower price, and keep the offer open as a possible replacement while the partners decide.
C. Judge the offer by what Halcyon has to deliver, air before the reserve ends, and by its cost from here, not money spent.
D. Send the offer to the partners as a cheaper way to finish the job, since it saves money, and let the board see the schedule after.

Quinn does it on the whiteboard in two columns. The 2.3 billion goes on neither, because it's spent either way. Stay: 310 to finish. Switch: 185, plus what it costs to change, which is most of the rest, and it comes to 303. Seven million cheaper. Then the line that decides it. A minimum energy transfer leaving in February arrives on November 4, 2063, sixty one days after the agency's own number for the air runs out, with nobody aboard to install anything. Sam sends Osterhout the whiteboard and one sentence: the cheaper flight saves seven million and delivers a plant to a station that can't use it. He asks that the offer go in the record, declined for this mission, and that Kittiwake be invited to bid on the station's resupply after arrival. Osterhout writes back. Agreed. I did like the price.

That's a go. Value based delivery means judging options by the value they deliver against what they cost from here. Sunk costs don't count either way, and an option that misses the benefit delivers nothing at any price.
Decision eight. Ahead of the board.

Monday, October 30. 7:10 AM. Rafa's team had closed its sprint on Friday with a demo of the workaround software: the conditioning cycle, MOIV-2's close at cutoff, the new crew display, all of it running on the bench. The demo had gone well. The work was CR 62-311's, line for line, as the board had approved it.

Thandi Mokoena's note was the first thing in Sam's inbox. Build 11.4 contains a change not in CR 62-311: a 30 millisecond pre close pulse on MOIV-1 at cutoff. Not requested, not analyzed, not approved. It is loaded for Wednesday's ground runs.

Rafa came in at 7:30 with his coffee and didn't sit down. We saw it in the traces. A short pulse before the close might seat the poppet before it gets a chance to chatter. It's twelve lines. It's in a sprint, which is where ideas are supposed to go. And it might be the thing that fixes it.
It might. Wednesday's runs were on the lot sample valve Aldergrove had trucked up from Pueblo, and they were the board's evidence for December.
A. Take the pulse out of the build quietly and let the matter drop, so the approved work isn't held up by an argument about it.
B. Pull the pulse from Wednesday's load, write it up as a change request of its own, and test only what the board approved.
C. Report the team to the readiness board for working outside the approved scope, so everyone can see that the process is enforced.
D. Keep the pulse in the build, since it came out of the data and the team is empowered to improve its own work inside a sprint.

Rafa takes it better than Sam expected. It's a good idea. I'd still like it to be a decided one. The pulse comes out of Wednesday's load in an hour, and Thandi's team verifies the build against CR 62-311 line by line. Rafa writes the pulse up as CR 62-334, with the traces that suggested it and a test that could prove it, and it goes on the change board's next agenda. That afternoon the configuration record, the procedure, and the crew's training plan are brought up to the approved build, and Quinn posts the status of both changes on the program page: one approved and in work, one proposed. Wednesday's runs test exactly what the board approved.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Implement only approved changes, and update the documentation to match. A good idea from the team is welcome as a proposed change. The backlog can change freely inside a sprint; a baseline governance approved can't.

Tuesday, October 31. 8:00 AM. The Mars Surface Accord had eleven signatures on it, all eleven of the ARA's partners, and a science council that met twice a year. In June the council had adopted a rule, and it took effect tomorrow. Nobody at Tallgrass had read it until the ARA's sustainability office forwarded it at 7:52 with one word in the subject line: Lander?

MARS SURFACE ACCORD SCIENCE COUNCIL RULE 14 (EXTRACT). EFFECTIVE NOVEMBER 1, 2062.. ANY LANDER LAUNCHED ON OR AFTER THAT DATE WHOSE LANDING SITE IS WITHIN 10 KM OF A PROTECTED SAMPLE SITE IN THE JEZERO DELTA SHALL HAVE ITS SURFACE CONTACT HARDWARE DRY HEAT TREATED AND SHALL CARRY A BIOBURDEN ASSAY CERTIFIED BY THE COUNCIL.
The Breather's lander would set down at Ares Station, in the old delta, 3.2 kilometers from the nearest protected site. Launch 3 was Thursday, November 16.

Hana did the first estimate on the back of the email. If it's the footpads and the gear, it's the oven, thirty hours at temperature plus the time to bag it and bring it up and down and put it back. Five days. Two for the assay. Seven on the lander's path.
Garrett had a solution by nine, which was to launch before tomorrow. Hale's office had another by ten, which was to ask for an exemption, because it was a rescue.
A. Ask the council for a formal exemption for a rescue flight, and keep the lander's processing as it is while the council decides.
B. Treat the rule as not applying to Halcyon, since its contracts and its launch license were signed long before the rule existed.
C. Confirm with the council what the rule asks of this lander, put the work into the plan through change control, and replan.
D. Pull launch 3 ahead of November 1, so that the lander is in orbit before the new rule applies to anything that launches.

Hana and the ARA's sustainability office are on a call with the council's secretariat by noon. The rule is narrower than its headline: the footpads and the gear struts, the parts that touch the ground, and nothing above them. Thirty hours at 112 degrees Celsius in a sealed bag, the way the old landers that went looking for life on Mars were done, plus the time to bag, ramp, cool, and reinstall: five days. Then two for the assay. CR 62-341 goes to the change board on Wednesday with the seven days on it and the reason in one line. The station's medical officer, who once asked in a packet who decided things, writes back that the colony would rather not be the first people on Mars to contaminate the delta, and thank you.

Exactly right. When the external environment changes, confirm what the change requires of your project, assess its impact on scope and schedule, and bring it in through change control. A rule you'd rather not meet is still a rule.
Thursday, November 2. 7:00 AM. CR 62-341 had come out of the change board on Wednesday approved, seven days and all.

Delphine had been clear about the range. Launch 3 had a slot on Thursday, November 16. The next one the range could give a heavy lifter was Thursday, November 30, fourteen days later, and fourteen days was more than the plan had in front of the crew launch. After that it came out of the window.

Quinn had the lander's path on the whiteboard. From the start of the lander's processing on Wednesday, October 25, to the slot there were twenty two days. Before the rule, the work on the path had come to twenty, two days of float. With the oven and the assay it was twenty seven. Five short.

LAUNCH 3 LANDER PATH TO THE NOV 16 SLOT CRASH OPTIONS MILLIONS). DRY HEAT, FOOTPADS AND GEAR: 5 DAYS. CANNOT SHORTEN.. BIOBURDEN ASSAY: 2 DAYS. CANNOT SHORTEN.. LANDER PROPELLANT LOAD: 4 DAYS. SECOND CREW: 1 DAY FOR 0.6.. BREATHER STOWAGE AND CLOSEOUT: 5 DAYS. EXTRA HANDS: UP TO 2 DAYS AT 1.0 A DAY.. INTEGRATED SYSTEMS TEST: 3 DAYS. COMPRESSED: 1 DAY FOR 0.8.. ENCAPSULATION AND MATE: 6 DAYS. SECOND SHIFT: UP TO 2 DAYS AT 0.7 A DAY.. ROLLOUT AND LAUNCH: 2 DAYS. FIXED.
Corinne had her legal pad. Her people had done a second shift in September, after a hurricane, and some of them had liked the money and some of them were tired.
A. Buy the five days on the lander's path where they cost least per day, leave the integrated test alone, and confirm the slot.
B. Shorten the oven time to fit the slot, since the council cares about the result and thirty hours is a generous figure anyway.
C. Give up the 16th, take the 30th, and tell Hale that the crew launch moves by however much the float can't absorb after that.
D. Run the oven at the same time as the Breather's stowage, in parallel, so that the days come back without spending any money.

Quinn ranks the work by cost per day on the whiteboard. A second propellant crew buys one day for 0.6 million. A second shift on encapsulation buys two at 0.7 a day. Two more come out of the Breather's stowage at a million each, with Paloma's people flown in from Albuquerque to help, because they know where everything in it goes. Five days, 4.0 million. The integrated systems test would have been cheaper by two hundred thousand dollars for its one day, and nobody suggests it twice. Corinne asks every person on the new shifts whether they want the hours before she posts a roster. On Friday Delphine confirms the 16th with the range.

That's a go. To recover schedule, crash the critical path activities with the lowest cost per day first, and don't compress the tests that tell you the work is right. Then confirm the new dates with the people who own them.

Friday, November 3. Quinn had started a wall in the program room the week of the broadcast, without telling anybody, on the long blank stretch between the window and the door. By Friday it had four sheets on it, one for each thing that had walked in from outside in four weeks.

A leaked record. An election. A company's offer. A rule. Under each, in her small hand, a date: when it could first have been known. The election had been on a calendar for a year. The rule had been published in June. Kittiwake had flown its tug twice, in public, and talked about Mars on its website. Only the leak had come with no warning, and even that, Quinn had written, had been sitting in somebody's drawer for three years waiting for a bad week.
Three of four, she said. We could have seen three of four coming. We weren't looking. Nobody's job was looking.
Under the rule she'd pinned the council's June press release, which had been on its website for four months.
A. Leave the outside world to the ARA's policy and public affairs offices, since elections and rules are the sponsor's business.
B. Set up a standing scan by category, each with an owner, reviewed every two weeks, feeding what it finds to risks and backlog.
C. Have Quinn scan the whole outside world herself every week and brief the leads, since she's seen most of this coming already.
D. Buy a news monitoring service that sends the team every story mentioning Halcyon, so that nothing outside is ever missed again.

Quinn puts six columns on the wall: political, economic, social, technological, legal, environmental. Each gets an owner who already watches it for a living. Peg takes legal and economic. The ARA's liaison takes political. Hana and the sustainability office share environmental, Rafa takes technological, and Frances agrees to tell them what the families are hearing, which is social and better than any poll. Every other Friday, fifteen minutes, each owner names one thing that changed and whether it touches the risk register or the backlog. The first review finds two: a second partner's election in March, and a refinery fire on the Gulf Coast that's put liquid methane up eighteen percent for the winter.

Good. That's what I'd want on my loop. Evaluating the external environment is continual: survey changes by category, assess and prioritize their impact on scope and backlog, and review on a cadence, with owners who'd notice.
Monday, November 6. The integrated plan on the program's shared drive was version 14, dated September 11, the day the Cape reopened. It described a world before the feed.

Since then: CR 62-311, approved in part by the board, with Aldergrove's lot started and the workaround in ground runs. CR 62-334, Rafa's pulse, proposed and on the change board's agenda. CR 62-341, the oven and the assay, seven days on the lander's path, bought back for 4.0 million to hold the 16th. Partner 09's sixteen million, with the committee's answer still to come. Kittiwake's offer, declined for this mission and on file. A communications agreement on a whiteboard, written in pen where the crew had asked.
Hale's office wanted a new plan before launch 3. Garrett wanted a new schedule, which he said was the same thing.
A. Fold every change into the integrated plan, check the whole of it for new dependencies and gaps, and confirm it's still worth doing.
B. Update the schedule with every change and reissue it, since the dates are what the partners and the board look at first anyway.
C. Have each lead update their own part of the plan this week, since each knows better than anyone what has changed in their area.
D. Freeze the plan until launch 3 has flown, so that the team can work without the distraction of yet another revision arriving.

It takes Quinn three days and every lead for an hour each. Folding it all together finds two things nobody could see from inside one change. The workaround's ground runs and the lander's last week both wanted Corinne's same four certified technicians. And if the closeout work were rephased, the station's spares training would land after the crew left Earth. Both are fixed on paper before anybody is standing in the wrong place. The last page asks whether it's still worth doing, and Quinn answers with the measure the program exists for: the margin in days, on the agency's number and the station's own, against the arrival. It is. Version 15 goes to the board on Thursday with a change log in front of it.

Exactly right. Maintaining the integrated plan means bringing every approved change into one plan, assessing the whole for dependencies and gaps, and checking that it still delivers the value it exists for.

Thursday, November 9. 10:40 PM. The workaround's ground runs had gone on at night all week, because the cell and its people were cheaper at night and Wendell was better. They were running at Stand 2, on the lot sample valve Aldergrove had trucked up from Pueblo in October, and Sam was in the blockhouse with Quinn, because he'd started coming out for them and couldn't have said why.
The load was the one the board had approved, verified line by line, and nothing else. Rafa's pulse was on the change board's agenda for Tuesday, with a test written for it.

The month was on a sheet in his notebook. Frances's call was Friday at ten, the fifth one. She'd started them by reading out what the families were hearing, so he'd know what to correct. Kittiwake had written to say it would bid on the station's resupply. Launch 3 was a week out, on the 16th, bought back a day at a time.

He'd answered Ada's log forty three the night he got home, at the kitchen table, in his own chair. He'd told her what he'd told Greaves, and the part he hadn't, about the gray bar down the side of the scan.
It had been five weeks of the outside walking in, and most of it, he thought, had gone through the door it was supposed to. He knew better than to trust that much.

Cycle after cycle came back under four milliseconds, with the conditioning cycle ahead of the close and MOIV-2 shutting behind it like a second hand on a door. Twice, on the third cycle after a long soak, the trace showed a small ripple about two milliseconds after the poppet lifted. Sam had seen that ripple once before, at the Cape, in September, beside a seven.
At 10:52 Wendell stood up from the propulsion console to look at something on the far screen, put his hand out for the back of the chair, and missed it.

Quinn got to him first. He was on the blockhouse floor on his side, awake, saying he was fine in a voice that wasn't. Arlo called it in from the stand. The ambulance came up the gravel road with its lights on and no siren, because Arlo had told them there was nobody out there to wake, and the pronghorn in the ditch didn't move.

At 2:10 AM a doctor at the hospital in Aurora said low blood pressure, and a heart that needed a better look, and that he was fine for tonight. They also said that seventy one year old men shouldn't be working nights on a prairie in November. Wendell said he'd been told.
Sam sat in the chair by the bed with his jacket still on. Wendell looked at the ceiling for a while.
This is the last one, Sam. I'll see it to December. Then I'm done. I've been done since 2035. I kept forgetting.

Sam didn't argue. He thought about what was in that bed. How a seat sounded when it was lying. Which ripple was ice and which wasn't. The thing Wendell had heard in 2034, and in 2059, and at 10:52 tonight, when he'd stood up to look. Some of it was in procedures now. The part that mattered had never been written down by anybody, because nobody had ever asked him the right way, and he'd never offered.
Over the high bay doors, fifteen miles east, the clock said 100.
